newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia poll breakthrough remains elusive.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia poll breakthrough remains elusive.

text.p: Intense diplomatic efforts have so far failed to resolve an impasse threatening Bosnian local elections due next month, Western officials said on Monday.

The Serbs have said they could boycott the polls because of rising tension in some areas of Bosnia and dissatisfaction with the international body running the elections, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
OSCE spokesman David Foley said consultations with the Serbs continued over the weekend and while progress was made, no agreement was reached.

Discussions were held with officials close to Biljana Plavsic, the hardline president of the Serb republic in Bosnia, to try to persuade her to drop her opposition to OSCE-supervised municipal elections set for November 23 and 24.
"It is an intensive diplomatic exercise. We are consulting, coordinating and cooperating with all sides," Foley told a news conference.
"We believe that things are moving in the right direction but we have not reached closure on the issue."

Foley said the OSCE's Bosnian mission chief, Robert Frowick of the United States, still wanted to hold the elections as planned, and issued a warning that postponement could mean the polls might have to be held without international supervision.
"Postponement is under any circumstances unlikely," Foley said.
"The choice is to hold municipal elections now, as scheduled, under international supervision or there is a risk that they will not be held at all under international supervision," he said.
The local elections follow national polls for a presidency and parliament held on September 14.
Western officials urged the Bosnian Serb member of the rotating three-man presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, to drop his opposition to signing the required oath of loyalty to Bosnian statehood.

Krajisnik came to central Sarajevo on Saturday for the first time since his forces stopped besieging the capital and held talks at their embassies with U.S. envoy John Kornblum and German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel.

The Bosnian Serb leader returned to the village of Pale, his mountain headquarters outside the city, still refusing to sign the declaration which amounts to a renunciation of Serb war aims to carve out a separate state.
Colum Murphy, spokesman for international mediator Carl Bildt, appealed to Krajisnik to "behave presidentially" and join in the work of the presidency.

"Instead, we see President Krajisnik entering through side doors having already been invited to the main door, groping in the half light for the light switch and casting around to find his rightful seat," Murphy said.
